targets.title: Escaping the Evils of Centralized Control with Self-certifying Pathnames
targets.authors: David Mazières, M. Frans Kaashoek
targets.why_needed: Defines the self-certifying name construction (name = hash of the holder's public key, holder signs the binding to current content/state) that every later self-certifying-identity and self-certifying-content-address scheme reuses; the formal precursor to IPNS-style naming this repo's evidence file needs before evaluating any naming-ledger alternative.

targets.title: Names: Decentralized, Secure, Human-Meaningful: Choose Two (the original statement of Zooko's triangle)
targets.authors: Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn
targets.why_needed: Original formulation of the three-property naming trilemma (decentralized, secure, human-meaningful — pick two) that every naming-ledger, self-certifying-name, and 'escapes Zooko's triangle' claim in this domain must be checked against; not a peer-reviewed paper, so any measured claim from it must stay labeled accordingly.

targets.title: CONIKS: Bringing Key Transparency to End Users
targets.authors: Marcela S. Melara, Aaron Blankstein, Joseph Bonneau, Edward W. Felten, Michael J. Freedman
targets.why_needed: Foundational key-transparency design: a verifiable Merkle-tree directory of name-to-key bindings, signed and chained epoch-to-epoch, letting a user detect a substituted key by monitoring only their own entry. Every later key-transparency system (SEEMless, Merkle^2, Parakeet) states its own contribution as an improvement against this baseline, so its cost figures (proof size, update latency) are the comparison point.

targets.title: SEEMless: Secure End-to-End Encrypted Messaging with less</> Trust
targets.authors: Melissa Chase, Apoorvaa Deshpande, Esha Ghosh, Harjasleen Malvai
targets.why_needed: States a key-transparency directory built for update throughput at messaging-provider scale (verifiable random functions for hidden lookups, batched Merkle updates), positioned directly against CONIKS's design; needed for the throughput-versus-privacy comparison among key-transparency candidates.

targets.title: Parakeet: Practical Key Transparency for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging
targets.authors: Harjasleen Malvai, Lefteris Kokoris-Kogias, Alberto Sonnino, Esha Ghosh, Ercan Öztürk, Kevin Lewi, Sean F. Lawlor
targets.why_needed: Written by the WhatsApp/Meta key-transparency team; extends CONIKS/SEEMless with bounded-size compaction and threshold-witness signing at billions-of-updates-per-week scale, and is the paper the deployed WhatsApp Auditable Key Directory (announced by Meta engineering, April 2023, publicly audited by Cloudflare from 2023) implements. Needed as the deployed-scale evidence point for the key-transparency component decision.

targets.title: Merkle^2: A Low-Latency Transparency Log System
targets.authors: Yuncong Hu, Kian Hooshmand, Harika Kalidhindi, Seung Jin Yang, Raluca Ada Popa
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
targets.why_needed: A two-dimensional Merkle-tree construction (one dimension over identities, one over time) aimed at reducing key-transparency proof latency; the specific alternative to CONIKS/Parakeet's single-tree-per-epoch design and the source for whichever latency figures decide between them.

targets.title: An Empirical Study of Namecoin and Lessons for Decentralized Namespace Design
targets.authors: Harry A. Kalodner, Miles Carlsten, Paul Ellenbogen, Joseph Bonneau, Arvind Narayanan
targets.venue: Workshop on the Economics of Information Security (WEIS)
targets.why_needed: Independent measurement of a deployed blockchain naming ledger: how many names were actually registered, squatted, or left unused, and what that implies for consensus-secured human-readable naming as an approach to the Zooko's-triangle third property. Needed as the deployment-scale counterpoint to any theoretical naming-ledger proposal.

targets.title: A Censorship-Resistant, Privacy-Enhancing and Fully Decentralized Name System
targets.authors: Matthias Wachs, Martin Schanzenbach, Christian Grothoff
targets.venue: International Conference on Cryptology and Network Security (CANS)
targets.why_needed: Defines the GNU Name System: per-user private name-to-key mappings with no global consensus and no global uniqueness, the structural opposite of Namecoin/ENS/Handshake's ledger-consensus approach to the same trilemma corner. Needed to state the consensus-free naming alternative's cost (each user resolves a different meaning for the same name) as fact rather than by assumption.

targets.title: Challenges in Decentralized Name Management: The Case of ENS
targets.authors: Pengcheng Xia, Haoyu Wang, Zhou Yu, Xinyu Liu, Xiapu Luo, Guoai Xu, Gareth Tyson
targets.why_needed: First large-scale measurement of the Ethereum Name Service naming ledger, reporting security problems specific to a blockchain-consensus naming design (not present in classic DNS) alongside legacy DNS-style problems it inherits. Needed as the empirical test of whether a ledger-based naming system that claims to give a readable, secure, decentralized name actually delivers all three at deployment scale, rather than only in the design document.

targets.title: Handshake: A Decentralized, Permissionless Naming Protocol Compatible with the Domain Name System
targets.authors: Handshake project (collective; whitepaper unattributed to named individuals in the retrieved copy)
targets.why_needed: Describes a proof-of-work blockchain used only to secure the DNS root zone (top-level names), leaving lower DNS levels to existing infrastructure — a narrower-scope alternative to Namecoin/ENS's whole-namespace ledger. Not a peer-reviewed source; any number from it enters the evidence file only as project-stated design intent, not as a measured fact, per the citing-abstracts rule extended to project documents.

targets.title: Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) v1.0
targets.authors: W3C Credentials Community Group / DID Working Group (Manu Sporny, Amy Guy, Markus Sabadello, Drummond Reed, editors)
targets.why_needed: The normative specification of the DID URI scheme and its resolution/verification data model, which every decentralized-identifier implementation (including the DID methods used by verifiable-credential and self-sovereign-identity systems in this domain) must conform to for interoperability. Needed as the primary definitional source rather than a secondary description of DIDs.

targets.title: Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0
targets.authors: W3C Verifiable Credentials Working Group (Manu Sporny, Ted Thibodeau Jr., Ivan Herman, Michael B. Jones, Gabe Cohen, editors)
targets.why_needed: The normative data model for verifiable credentials (issuer, subject, claims, proof) that BBS+-based and other anonymous-credential schemes in this domain implement as a concrete credential format. Needed as the primary definitional source before evaluating any anonymous-credential proof system built to issue or present credentials in this format.

targets.title: Secure Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Based Cryptosystems
targets.authors: Rosario Gennaro, Stanislaw Jarecki, Hugo Krawczyk, Tal Rabin
targets.why_needed: Identifies a flaw in the earlier Pedersen distributed-key-generation protocol (a rushing adversary can bias the output key) and gives the corrected construction, making this the correctness-baseline DKG protocol that every threshold-signature or threshold-decryption scheme for group identity keys must be checked against. Needed before selecting any DKG for a guardian-quorum key-recovery or threshold-signing identity component.

targets.title: Non-Interactive and Information-Theoretic Secure Verifiable Secret Sharing
targets.authors: Torben P. Pedersen
targets.why_needed: Gives the verifiable secret-sharing scheme (participants can check their share is consistent with a public commitment, without revealing the secret) that distributed key generation and guardian-quorum social recovery both build on. Needed as the mechanism a later synthesis cites when a key-recovery or threshold-key-generation component claims share verifiability.

targets.title: How to Share a Secret
targets.authors: Adi Shamir
targets.why_needed: Defines (k,n)-threshold secret sharing via polynomial interpolation over a finite field: any k of n shares reconstruct the secret, fewer than k reveal nothing information-theoretically. This is the arithmetic every guardian-quorum key-recovery scheme in this domain (and every threshold-signature DKG) reduces to; needed as the primitive-level citation beneath both.

targets.title: FROST: Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures
targets.authors: Chelsea Komlo, Ian Goldberg
targets.why_needed: A threshold Schnorr signature scheme requiring only one round of signer communication in the common case (versus prior threshold-Schnorr protocols' multiple rounds), with a security proof against Boneh-Drijvers-Neven-style rogue-key attacks; the round-count figure and the security model it targets are the numbers a later synthesis needs when comparing threshold-signing latency against BLS threshold signatures. Standardized afterward as IETF RFC 9591 (2024), which is the deployment-adoption signal for this specific scheme over its predecessors.

targets.title: Short Signatures from the Weil Pairing
targets.authors: Dan Boneh, Ben Lynn, Hovav Shacham
targets.why_needed: Introduces the BLS signature scheme: a pairing-based signature shorter than DSA/Schnorr at equivalent security, and the only common signature scheme whose signatures on different messages by different keys can be combined into one constant-size aggregate that a verifier checks against the list of (message, public key) pairs. This aggregation property is the reason every threshold- and multi-signature scheme in this domain (Boldyreva, BDN, FROST as contrast) is built on or compared against BLS.

targets.title: Threshold Signatures, Multisignatures and Blind Signatures Based on the Gap-Diffie-Hellman-Group Signature Scheme
targets.authors: Alexandra Boldyreva
targets.why_needed: Gives the threshold and multi-signature variants of BLS with a formal security proof, so any (k,n)-threshold BLS identity-key scheme in this domain traces its unforgeability guarantee to this paper rather than to an informal extension of the base BLS scheme.

targets.title: Aggregate and Verifiably Encrypted Signatures from Bilinear Maps
targets.authors: Dan Boneh, Craig Gentry, Ben Lynn, Hovav Shacham
targets.why_needed: Gives the aggregate-signature construction proper (n signatures on n distinct messages from n distinct keys compressed to one signature of the same size as a single BLS signature), distinct from the threshold case in Boldyreva 2003 (n signers on one message). Needed because a group-membership or governance-quorum identity feature that batches many different signers' distinct attestations into one verification cost depends on this construction, not on threshold BLS.

targets.title: Simple Schnorr Multi-Signatures with Applications to Bitcoin
targets.authors: Gregory Maxwell, Andrew Poelstra, Yannick Seurin, Pieter Wuille
targets.why_needed: MuSig: an interactive (multi-round) Schnorr multi-signature scheme with a rogue-key-attack proof, on ordinary elliptic-curve groups with no pairing requirement — the non-pairing alternative to BLS aggregation for combining several identity keys' signatures into one. Needed as the pairing-versus-no-pairing tradeoff evidence (round count added versus pairing-library dependency removed) for the multi-signature component decision.

targets.title: Compact Multi-Signatures for Smaller Blockchains
targets.authors: Dan Boneh, Manu Drijvers, Gregory Neven
targets.why_needed: Gives a pairing-based multi-signature ("BDN") that removes the interactive key-aggregation-commitment round earlier BLS-based multi-signature schemes needed to block rogue-key attacks, at the cost of a proof-of-possession requirement per key at registration time. Needed as the specific improvement-over-earlier-BLS-multisig figure (round count removed, one-time proof-of-possession added) that a synthesis decision between MuSig, plain threshold BLS, and this scheme must cite.

targets.title: Short Group Signatures
targets.authors: Dan Boneh, Xavier Boyen, Hovav Shacham
targets.why_needed: Introduces the BBS group signature scheme (a member proves membership in a group and signs a message without revealing which member, under a group manager who can revoke anonymity), the direct algebraic predecessor of the BBS+ signature scheme used for anonymous and zero-knowledge credentials. Needed before evaluating any BBS+-based verifiable-credential proposal, because BBS+'s change from this scheme (dropping the group-manager de-anonymization capability, adding multi-message signing) is the entire point of the later construction.

targets.title: Anonymous Attestation Using the Strong Diffie-Hellman Assumption Revisited
targets.authors: Jan Camenisch, Manu Drijvers, Anja Lehmann
targets.venue: International Conference on Trust and Trustworthy Computing (TRUST)
targets.why_needed: The paper that formalizes and proves security for what the field now calls BBS+: a signature scheme on a vector of messages, from which the holder proves knowledge of a signature and selectively discloses a subset of the signed messages in zero knowledge, with a formal unforgeability and anonymity proof the original informal 'BBS+' folklore construction lacked. This is the citation a verifiable-credential or selective-disclosure identity component needs before adopting BBS+ as its signature primitive.

targets.title: SoK: Anonymous Credentials
targets.authors: Saqib A. Kakvi, Keith M. Martin, Colin Putman, Elizabeth A. Quaglia
targets.why_needed: Systematization of Knowledge unifying the anonymous-credential literature (CL signatures, BBS+, U-Prove, idemix and their selective-disclosure and unlinkability properties) under one comparison framework. Needed as the entry point for choosing among anonymous-credential constructions with a stated, citable basis for the comparison rather than an ad hoc one.

targets.title: SoK: Anonymous Credentials for Digital Identity Wallets
targets.authors: Christian Bormann, Anja Lehmann
targets.venue: Security Standardisation Research (SSR); extended version IACR ePrint 2026
targets.why_needed: A 2025 follow-up SoK specifically scoped to the credential schemes under active standardization for government and EU digital-identity wallets (which constrains the anonymous-credential design space differently than the 2023 general SoK). Needed to check whether the credential scheme selected for this architecture's identity layer matches or diverges from what deployed-wallet standardization is converging on, and why.

targets.title: A Survey on Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials
targets.authors: Carlo Mazzocca, Abbas Acar, A. Selcuk Uluagac, Rebecca Montanari, Paolo Bellavista, Mauro Conti
targets.venue: IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials (arXiv preprint 2024, journal version 2025)
targets.why_needed: Surveys the DID/verifiable-credential ecosystem (methods, resolution infrastructure, wallet architectures, trust models) as a whole rather than the credential cryptography alone. Needed as the systems-level complement to the Kakvi/Bormann cryptographic SoKs when this domain's evidence file states what a DID-based identity layer requires from the rest of the architecture (resolver availability, revocation infrastructure).

targets.title: SoK: Self-Sovereign Digital Identities
targets.authors: Sushanth Ambati, Kainat Adeel, Jack Myers, Nikolay Ivanov
targets.venue: ACM Symposium on Access Control Models and Technologies (SACMAT)
targets.why_needed: The most recent (2026) Systematization of Knowledge on self-sovereign identity broadly, covering key management, recovery, and access-control aspects the two credential-focused SoKs above do not center. Needed to catch any 2025-2026 result on identity-key recovery or governance that supersedes what the earlier SoKs recorded, per the brief's explicit requirement to check for work superseding older results.

targets.title: Smart Contract-Based Social Recovery Wallet Management Scheme for Digital Assets
targets.authors: Konstantin Pedin, Mais Nijim, Mohammadamin Sameni
targets.why_needed: Gives a specific guardian-quorum key-recovery construction implemented as a smart contract (protected address, backup address, timelock, guardian threshold), one concrete point in the social-recovery design space this domain must evaluate against a non-blockchain-anchored recovery scheme built directly on Shamir/Pedersen secret sharing.

targets.title: Proof-of-Personhood: Redemocratizing Permissionless Cryptocurrencies
targets.authors: Maria Borge, Eleftherios Kokoris-Kogias, Philipp Jovanovic, Linus Gasser, Nicolas Gailly, Bryan Ford
targets.venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy Workshops (EuroS&PW)
targets.why_needed: Defines the pseudonym-party construction for proof of personhood: participants convene in person at an announced time and place and each receives exactly one anonymous token, with no participant identified. This is the foundational non-biometric, non-social-graph proof-of-personhood mechanism every later scheme (BrightID's social-graph substitute, Idena's synchronous-puzzle substitute, Worldcoin's biometric substitute) replaces one part of, so needed as the baseline every substitution is a deviation from.

targets.title: Who Watches the Watchmen? A Review of Subjective Approaches for Sybil-Resistance in Proof of Personhood Protocols
targets.authors: Divya Siddarth, Sergey Ivliev, Santiago Siri, Paula Berman
targets.why_needed: Critiques the social-graph and social-vouching family of proof-of-personhood schemes (the family BrightID and Proof of Humanity belong to) for depending on subjective human judgment calls at some point in the protocol, and analyzes the resulting exposure. Needed to extract the specific failure conditions of subjective-judgment-based proof of personhood as fact, separate from the paper's own framing of which tradeoffs are acceptable.

targets.title: Personhood Credentials: Artificial Intelligence and the Value of Privacy-Preserving Tools to Distinguish Who Is Real Online
targets.authors: Steven Adler, Zoë Hitzig, Shrey Jain, and 28 additional co-authors spanning OpenAI, Microsoft, MIT, and multiple civil-society and standards organizations
targets.why_needed: Cross-institutional framework paper defining 'personhood credential' as a general category (a credential attesting uniqueness and humanness without necessarily identifying which human) and setting out the design requirements the category must meet (unlinkability across issuances, revocability, no single-issuer capture). Needed as the framework this domain's specific proof-of-personhood systems (Worldcoin, BrightID, Idena, Proof of Humanity) are instances of, so their designs can be checked against a stated requirement set rather than against each other only.

targets.title: Personhood Credentials: Human-Centered Design Recommendation Balancing Security, Usability, and Trust
targets.authors: Ayae Ide, Tanusree Sharma
targets.why_needed: Systematically compares deployed proof-of-personhood systems (BrightID, Proof of Humanity, Gitcoin Passport, Idena among them named in the abstract) on usability and trust dimensions instead of cryptographic ones alone. Needed as the independent, cross-system comparison point rather than relying on each project's own claims about its own usability.

targets.title: BrightID Whitepaper
targets.authors: BrightID project (collective; not peer-reviewed)
targets.why_needed: Primary source for the BrightID mechanism itself: a social connection graph seeded by a small trusted-seed set, scored by a GroupSybilRank-style algorithm run over the graph. Needed because the Siddarth et al. and Ide/Sharma papers critique and compare BrightID but do not themselves fully specify its mechanism; any mechanism claim must come from this primary source, and any number from it is project-stated, not measured.

targets.title: Idena: Proof-of-Person Blockchain Technology Overview
targets.authors: Idena project (collective; not peer-reviewed)
targets.why_needed: Primary source for Idena's synchronous-ceremony proof of personhood: all candidates worldwide solve human-generated visual-reasoning puzzles ('flips') within one fixed global time window, so no single participant can complete two sessions. Needed as the mechanism description for the time-synchronization-based alternative to BrightID's social-graph and Worldcoin's biometric approaches; project-stated, not independently measured.

targets.title: World (Worldcoin) Whitepaper
targets.authors: Tools for Humanity (collective; not peer-reviewed)
targets.why_needed: Primary source for the biometric-iris proof-of-personhood mechanism (local iris-hash computation on a purpose-built device, zero-knowledge-proof-gated World ID issuance) that the personhood-credential framework papers and the Ide/Sharma comparison reference but do not themselves fully specify. Any exposure claim (device-manufacturer trust, hardware supply-chain requirement) must be traced to this primary source and kept labeled as project-stated design intent rather than an independently measured property.

targets.title: SPHINCS: Practical Stateless Hash-Based Signatures
targets.authors: Daniel J. Bernstein, Daira Hopwood, Andreas Hülsing, Tanja Lange, Ruben Niederhagen, Louiza Papachristodoulou, Michael Schneider, Peter Schwabe, Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn
targets.why_needed: First practical hash-based signature scheme requiring no signer-side state to track across signatures (a stateful hash-based scheme that reuses a one-time key pair breaks security, which rules out stateful schemes for a long-lived identity key with no reliable state-persistence guarantee across devices). Needed as the foundational construction before evaluating its 2019 successor for post-quantum identity-key signing.

targets.title: The SPHINCS+ Signature Framework
targets.authors: Andreas Hülsing, Denis Butin, Stefan-Lukas Gazdag, Joost Rijneveld, Aziz Mohaisen (framework paper; NIST submission led by Bernstein, Hülsing, and additional co-authors)
targets.why_needed: The improved, smaller-signature stateless hash-based scheme that became the basis for NIST's standardized post-quantum signature FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA). Needed as the specific post-quantum signature candidate for a long-lived identity key that requires no stored per-signature state and rests only on hash-function security (no lattice or pairing assumption), the most conservative security assumption among the post-quantum options in this domain.

targets.title: CRYSTALS-Dilithium: A Lattice-Based Digital Signature Scheme
targets.authors: Léo Ducas, Eike Kiltz, Tancrède Lepoint, Vadim Lyubashevsky, Peter Schwabe, Gregor Seiler, Damien Stehlé
targets.venue: IACR Transactions on Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems (TCHES)
targets.why_needed: A lattice-based (module-LWE/module-SIS) post-quantum signature scheme with smaller signatures and faster verification than SPHINCS+, at the cost of resting on a newer, less-studied hardness assumption and requiring the signer to track state-free but still larger keys; became the basis for NIST FIPS 204 (ML-DSA). Needed as the size/speed-versus-assumption-age tradeoff point against SPHINCS+ for the post-quantum identity-signature component decision.
